transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, um, my regular doctor sent me. He seems a bit concerned that my meal planning has gotten... well, too tight, I suppose. But honestly, as an operations research analyst, planning is just what I do. It's second nature. Actually, I was just working on this massive logistical model for a freight company the other day—fascinating stuff, really, trying to optimize their delivery routes when you have unpredictable weather patterns. Have you ever driven through Ohio in November? It is just dreadfully gray. 

But anyway, to me, my eating just feels like keeping things orderly. I keep breakfast to just a yogurt—usually that Greek kind, though they changed the lids recently and they are absolutely impossible to peel off without getting it all over your fingers. I really should write to the company about that. And then I just skip lunch if I’m busy with my spreadsheets, and make a very, very measured dinner. It just ensures the day stays orderly, you know? Like a good algorithm. I don't really see the problem.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight recently, or do you have concerns about your body shape or size?

Well, I suppose my weight has drifted down a bit more than my doctor likes. He fusses over it. But honestly, when I look at the chart, I still find myself thinking that a little lower would just be a cleaner, more manageable number. Like rounding down to a nice, neat integer. 

Speaking of integers, I was trying to explain the importance of clean data sets to my niece the other day. She’s in college now—studying art history, of all things. I have no earthly idea what she expects to do with that in this economy. We went to an exhibit last week at that museum downtown, the one with the absolutely dreadful parking garage? The spots are just incredibly narrow. I drive a standard sedan and I could barely get my door open. I ended up scuffing my good navy pumps on the concrete pillar just trying to squeeze out. Have you ever noticed how modern parking structures are completely un-optimized for actual human use? It’s a total failure of spatial planning, if you ask me. Whoever drafted those blueprints wasn't thinking about turning radiuses at all. 

But anyway... what were we saying? Oh, right, the doctor's scale. Yes, I just think a lower number is tidier.
Can you tell me more about why you choose to eat such small amounts and whether this is something that causes you distress or is tied to how you feel about yourself?

Well, it's... it's about control, I suppose. It doesn't distress me to eat small amounts, it distresses me when I *don't*. If I have a normal dinner, or heaven forbid, go to a restaurant, and the scale is up even a pound the next morning... I feel this sharp, awful panic. Like the whole system is breaking down and I've completely lost control, and I just have to correct it immediately the next day. 

Speaking of restaurants, my sister insisted on taking me to this new Italian place for my birthday last month. The noise level in there was just astronomical. They had these high, exposed industrial ceilings—very trendy, I know, but acoustically, it's a nightmare. The sound waves just bounce everywhere. I couldn't hear a word she was saying across the table. And the waiter kept interrupting us to ask if we wanted sparkling or still water, and he had this enormous pepper grinder that looked like a baseball bat. I mean, honestly, who needs that much pepper? I ended up just ordering a side salad because the menu was so overwhelming and the print was so tiny. I had to use the flashlight on my phone just to read the vinaigrette options. I don't know why they dim the lights so much, it's a restaurant, not a movie theater. 

But yes, that panic... it just feels like if I don't fix the number right away, everything is going to spiral out of order.
Do you ever feel that your eating habits or concerns about weight are interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Well, I wouldn't say it interferes with the important things. I still keep up with my analysis work perfectly fine, and I run all my errands. I do have to be quite structured about it, though. But I suppose... well, I have mostly stopped joining my friends for lunch or dinner after our monthly book club. It just completely throws off the plan I rely on, and it’s not worth the stress of trying to calculate the variables of whatever they decide to order. 

Actually, the book club has been reading some very questionable selections lately anyway. Last month, Brenda—she’s the one who always brings those awful store-bought cookies—she picked this historical fiction novel set in 18th-century France. And the author clearly did absolutely zero research on the agricultural practices of the time. They had a character harvesting tomatoes in early spring! In Paris! It completely ruined the suspension of disbelief for me. I spent half the meeting trying to explain the crop rotation cycles of the era, but they just wanted to talk about the romance plot. Which, frankly, was just as poorly constructed. The pacing was entirely off. 

But yes, I just tell them I have to get back to my spreadsheets. It’s much easier than trying to manage the unpredictability of a restaurant menu.
Do you have a strong fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you are currently at a lower weight than your doctor considers healthy?

Well, I wouldn't call it a fear of becoming fat, exactly. That sounds so... emotional. It's more of a very strong preference for efficiency. A fear of the numbers creeping up and ruining the baseline I've established. If the weight goes up, it means my intake calculations were wrong, and I abhor an error in the data. 

Speaking of data errors, you wouldn't believe the absolute mess I had to untangle at work on Tuesday. One of the junior analysts—I think his name is Kevin, he always wears these terribly scuffed loafers—he had completely misaligned the columns on the Q3 supply chain projection. He had the freight costs merging into the warehousing overhead. I mean, it was a disaster. If I hadn't caught it, they would have presented that report to the regional director. And the regional director is this very severe woman who insists on everything being printed out on physical paper. Who prints spreadsheets in 2023? You have to tape the pages together just to see the quarterly progression. It's incredibly inefficient. I spent three hours reformatting the entire workbook just so it wouldn't look like a patchwork quilt when she printed it. 

But yes, to answer your question... I just don't like it when the scale goes up. It means the system isn't working the way I designed it to.
Do you ever exercise, fast, or do anything else to make up for the food you eat or to control your weight?

Well, I don't really do anything extreme like fasting for days or anything like that. I just stick to the schedule. If I miscalculate, I just adjust the next day's intake. It's just basic mathematics, really. 

Though, honestly, speaking of mathematics, I was trying to explain this very simple concept to my neighbor the other day. He was trying to figure out how much fertilizer he needed for his lawn, and he was just guessing! Throwing handfuls of it everywhere. I told him he needed to calculate the square footage and divide by the coverage rate on the bag, but he just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. And his lawn is a complete disaster anyway, it's half crabgrass. I don't understand why people don't just take a systematic approach to these things. It saves so much time and effort in the long run. He also leaves his recycling bin out for three days after pickup, which is a violation of the HOA bylaws, but nobody seems to enforce anything around here anymore. 

But no, I don't do any of those drastic things you mentioned to make up for food. I just keep the numbers balanced.
Would you say that you have a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you know you're currently at a lower weight than your doctor considers healthy?

I know we just touched on this, but... well, yes, if I'm being perfectly honest. If the scale is up even a single pound after a normal dinner or a restaurant meal, I do feel this... this sharp panic. It just feels like I’ve completely lost control of the variables, and I absolutely have to correct it the next day. 

Restaurant meals are just impossible to calculate anyway. I actually had to go to my sister's retirement dinner last Thursday at this Italian place downtown. The floor plan was an absolute nightmare. They had the waitstaff crossing directly through the main dining traffic just to get from the kitchen to the patio. It's a massive logistical bottleneck! I watched our waiter—who kept forgetting to refill the water glasses, by the way—collide with a busboy twice. Twice! If management had just implemented a simple circular routing system for the staff, they could increase their table turnover rate by at least fifteen percent. It’s not difficult to figure out. 

My sister didn't even notice the chaos, of course. She was just going on and on about her pension options. Which she hasn't diversified at all, despite my repeated advice. She just leaves it all in a default target-date fund that is far too conservative for the current inflation rate. I offered to build her a forecasting model, but she said she didn't want to look at a spreadsheet at her own party. 

But yes, if I eat in that kind of unpredictable environment and the scale is up the next morning, the panic is quite intense. I just have to fix the numbers immediately.
Do you ever feel that your weight or shape has a significant impact on how you see yourself or your sense of worth?

Well, yes... I suppose it does. I mean, I know I'm an older woman, I'm sixty-three, I'm certainly not trying to look like a twenty-something on a magazine cover. But I still judge how well I'm handling myself, how disciplined I am, by whether my waist and hips look contained in my clothes. If things feel loose and sharp, I know I'm operating efficiently. 

Speaking of clothes, I took a few of my blazers to the dry cleaner on Maple Street last week, and the owner—I think his name is George—has completely reorganized his intake system, and not for the better. He used to have a very logical alphabetical tagging system, but now he's color-coding by the day of the week, which makes absolutely no sense because what happens if someone drops off on a Tuesday but requests a rush order for Wednesday? The colors completely overlap and defeat the purpose of visual sorting. I tried to explain this to him while he was searching for my navy blazer—which took him five minutes, by the way—but he just waved me off. It's so frustrating to watch a perfectly good small business create its own inefficiencies. I almost offered to flowchart a new tagging process for him on the spot. 

But yes, to get back to what you were asking... if my clothes don't fit exactly the way they should, if my shape feels off, I definitely feel like I'm failing at maintaining my own standards.
Do you believe your concerns about eating and weight are primarily about maintaining control and discipline in your life, or are they more specifically about a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat?

Well, I suppose it's... it's a bit of both, isn't it? I mean, the control is paramount. If I can't control the input and the output, what can I control? But yes, the fear of the weight itself is definitely there. It's the physical manifestation of losing that control. If I see the number go up, or if I feel... heavier, it's terrifying. 

It's like when the city decided to change the traffic light sequencing on 4th Avenue last month. They completely ignored the peak flow data from the morning commute. I sat at my window with a stopwatch for three mornings in a row—just out of curiosity, really—and the idle time at the intersection of 4th and Elm has increased by an average of forty-two seconds per vehicle. Forty-two seconds! Multiply that by the hundreds of cars passing through, and the compounded loss of productivity is staggering. Not to mention the increased emissions. I actually drafted a letter to the city planner with a proposed optimization model using a simple queuing theory approach, but I haven't heard back. Typical municipal inefficiency. They just implement these changes without testing the variables, and suddenly everything is backed up and chaotic. 

So, yes, it's the fear of the chaos, the fear of the weight itself, because the weight means the system has broken down. The discipline is what keeps the fear at bay, I suppose.
Do you feel that your weight or shape is significantly different from how others might see it, or do you think others misunderstand how much you weigh?

Well, I don't really know. I haven't exactly taken a poll on how other people perceive my shape. I suppose my sister thinks I'm too thin, but she thinks everyone is too thin unless they're eating a second helping of her heavy cream pasta. 

Speaking of my sister, she finally called me back about the forecasting model I offered to build for her retirement fund. And you know what she said? She said she just trusts the bank's default algorithm. The default algorithm! I tried to explain to her that those algorithms are built on generalized actuarial tables that don't account for individual risk tolerance or localized inflation spikes. It's just lazy programming. I spent three hours over the weekend pulling historical data on target-date funds, just to show her the standard deviation in their returns during market downturns. The variance is honestly shocking if you actually look at the raw numbers. I even put it into a very clean, easy-to-read scatter plot for her, but she told me I was overcomplicating things. Overcomplicating! I'm trying to save her from a ten percent reduction in her purchasing power over the next decade! 

But anyway, I don't know if people misunderstand my weight. I just know what the numbers on my own scale say, and that's the only data point I really trust.
Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth depends heavily on your ability to control your weight or shape?

Well, yes, it really does. I think I touched on this earlier, but I know I’m an older woman now. I’m not trying to look young or pretend I'm in my twenties. But I absolutely still judge how well I’m handling myself—my whole sense of value, really—by whether my waist and hips look properly contained in my clothes. If they are, I know I'm doing a good job. 

Speaking of handling things properly, I actually had to go down to the post office yesterday to mail that scatter plot to my sister—since she refuses to open attachments on her tablet—and the queue management there is just an absolute disaster. They had three windows open, using a single-queue system. Now, theoretically, a single-queue system should minimize average wait times, but they had one teller processing passport applications! Passports take at least fifteen minutes. So the entire line kept stalling because their routing method didn't account for transaction-type variability. I stood there for twenty-five minutes just to mail one standard envelope. I actually tried to explain to the floor manager that they need a dedicated express line for transactions under two minutes—just basic triage—but he looked at me like I was speaking Greek. It’s staggering how people just accept such broken systems without trying to optimize them. 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, right, my self-worth. Yes, if my clothes don't feel right on my hips, I feel like I'm failing. It's just how I measure my own discipline.

Would you say that your fear of the scale going up is specifically about gaining weight, or is it more about the fact that it represents a loss of control, regardless of what the number actually means?

Well, it's... it's definitely about the weight itself, though the two are so intertwined, aren't they? If the scale is up even a pound—just one pound—after a normal dinner, or God forbid, a restaurant meal, I feel this sharp, sudden panic. It’s a very specific fear that I’ve gained weight, and it immediately translates into feeling like I’ve completely lost control. I just know I have to correct it the very next day. 

Restaurant meals are the absolute worst for that, actually. The variability in portion sizes and hidden sodium is a nightmare for data tracking. I was at this little Italian place on 8th Street last Thursday—just a small retirement dinner for a colleague from the firm—and the way they handled the seating arrangement was incredibly inefficient. They had pushed three rectangular tables together, but they didn't account for the structural pillars in the room, so the waitstaff had this massive bottleneck every time they tried to serve the middle section. I watched a busboy have to reroute his path five times just to clear the salad plates. It was agonizing to watch. I actually sketched out a more optimal floor plan on my napkin using a basic grid system to maximize flow efficiency. If they just angled the tables forty-five degrees, they could increase their table turnover rate by at least fifteen percent. I left the napkin under my water glass, hoping the manager might find it. 

But yes, the panic is real. If the number goes up, it means I'm getting heavier, and that means I have to fix it immediately.
Have you ever made yourself vomit, used laxatives or diuretics, or exercised excessively to control your weight or shape?

Well, no, I've never done anything like that. Making yourself sick or taking pills just seems so... biologically inefficient, honestly. And I don't exercise for hours on end either. 

I actually used to go to this local gym down the street, just for a normal amount of walking, but I had to cancel my membership last month because their equipment maintenance schedule was completely illogical. They would shut down a third of the treadmills for servicing at 6:00 AM on a Tuesday! That is absolute peak utilization hours. I tried to explain to the facility manager that if they just shifted their maintenance window to 2:00 PM on a Wednesday, they would reduce user disruption by at least eighty percent. It's just basic queueing theory. 

But he told me they contract out the maintenance and can't control the arrival times. Can you imagine? Signing a vendor contract without specifying service-level agreements for peak operating hours? It's just bad business. I couldn't bear to look at the bottleneck it caused every morning, watching people stand around waiting when they could be moving, so I just stopped going altogether. 

But, um... what was the first part of your question? Oh, right, laxatives and throwing up. No, no, I don't do any of that.

Would you say that your concerns about eating and weight have become so consuming that they affect how you experience most parts of your day, even when you're not actively eating or weighing yourself?

Well, they don't consume absolutely everything. I mean, I still keep up with all my analysis work just fine, and I run all my errands without any issue. 

Like, I still go to my book club every Thursday at the community center. Though, honestly, I don't know how much longer I can tolerate it because the woman who organizes the meetings—Susan—has absolutely no concept of time management or structured discussion. Last week, we were supposed to be analyzing a rather dense historical biography, and she let the group spend the first forty-five minutes talking about her daughter's kitchen renovation. Forty-five minutes! If she just implemented a simple timed agenda with five-minute speaking allocations per member, we could actually cover the thematic elements of the text efficiently. I even offered to create a tracking matrix for her so we could avoid the Pareto principle—you know, where twenty percent of the members do eighty percent of the talking—but she told me a book club is supposed to be "organic." Let me tell you, "organic" is just a polite code word for a completely unmanaged system. It drives me absolutely up the wall to sit there and watch the clock being wasted. 

But, um... I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, how my day is affected. Right. Well, I do still go to the meetings, but I’ve mostly stopped joining the friends for meals afterward. They always want to go out to eat once we finish, and I just can't do it anymore. It completely throws off the specific eating plan I rely on, and the anxiety of trying to fit their random restaurant choices into my structure is just too much. So I just skip the socializing part and go straight home.

Would you say that your concerns about food, weight, and control have become so rigid and all-consuming that they significantly interfere with your ability to enjoy or engage in life outside of these rules, even in areas that used to bring you pleasure?

Well, I don't know if I'd say it interferes with everything. I still do things I enjoy. But... I suppose it has changed how I approach certain situations. 

For instance, I used to really enjoy going to the botanical gardens on the weekends. It was so peaceful. But the last time I went, I noticed they completely overhauled their irrigation system, and it was just a disaster. They installed these rotary sprinklers in the rose garden, but the overlap coefficient was entirely miscalculated. You could see massive dry spots right next to areas that were completely oversaturated and pooling water. It’s a classic misapplication of hydro-zoning principles! If they had just mapped the soil absorption rates against the output volume of the sprinkler heads, they could have optimized the water distribution and probably saved themselves hundreds of dollars a month on their utility bill. I actually spent about an hour mapping out the dry zones on the back of my admission receipt to show them where the coverage gaps were. I tried to hand it to the groundskeeper, but he just looked at me like I was speaking a foreign language. 

It’s just... it’s so frustrating when systems aren't optimized. It ruins the whole experience for me. I haven't been back to the gardens since. 

But, um, to your point about the rules and food... I don't know. I guess I haven't really noticed it being all-consuming. I mean, I still have my routines. I'm just very structured, that's all.
Would you say that your concerns about food, weight, and control have caused you to avoid or withdraw from important social, occupational, or recreational activities that you used to participate in?

Well, I don't really think I'm withdrawing from everything. I mean, as I mentioned, I still keep up with my analysis work just fine, and I run my errands without any problem. I'm still functioning. 

But I did tell you about the book club, right? I still go to the meetings, even with Susan's terrible time management. But... yeah, I have stopped joining my friends for meals afterward. I just can't do it. Going out to a restaurant with them completely throws off the specific eating plan I rely on. The unpredictability of it all, trying to fit their random choices into my structure... it's just too much. So I just skip that part and go straight home. 

Speaking of going straight home, the traffic routing on the main avenue near the community center is another thing that just baffles me. They recently reprogrammed the traffic lights, and they completely ignored the staggered flow model. You hit a red light at 4th Street, and by the time it turns green, the light at 5th Street is already turning yellow. It creates this artificial bottleneck that backs up traffic for three blocks! If they just synchronized the lights based on a standard thirty-five mile-per-hour velocity vector, they could clear the entire corridor in half the time. I actually drafted a quick simulation model on my laptop to prove it and emailed it to the city's traffic engineering department. I haven't heard back, of course. Typical municipal inefficiency. 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, withdrawing from activities. Yeah, I mean, I guess I skip the meals after book club, but I'm still doing my work and my errands, so I wouldn't say I'm avoiding life.

Have you ever felt that your concerns about food, weight, or control have caused you to feel anxious, upset, or unable to function normally in situations where eating or body shape might be involved, even outside of your usual routine?

Anxious? Well, yes, I suppose I do. Especially if it involves a restaurant meal or something outside my normal parameters. Which, honestly, is usually an ordeal anyway because most restaurants have absolutely no idea how to manage their workflow. 

I was dragged to this new bistro downtown a few weeks ago when my sister visited, and their table turnover rate was just abysmal. They were clearly using a linear ticket system in the kitchen instead of parallel processing. You could literally see the servers standing at the pass, just waiting for one table's entire order to finish before the line cooks even started prepping the next ticket! It’s basic queuing theory. If they just implemented a staggered prep schedule based on standard cook times—you know, firing the proteins ten minutes before plating the cold appetizers—they could increase their throughput by at least thirty percent. I actually sketched a basic Gantt chart on my napkin to show the floor manager how they were bottlenecking their own service, but he just smiled and offered us a free dessert. Which I certainly didn't eat. 

But, um... where was I? Right, the anxiety. The thing is, if I do end up having a normal dinner like that, or a restaurant meal, the next morning is... well, it's very distressing. If I step on the scale and it's up even just a single pound, I feel this sharp panic. It just hits me that I’ve completely lost control of the variables, and I feel like I absolutely have to correct it the next day to get the numbers back to where they should be.

Would you say that your concerns about food, weight, or control have made it difficult for you to function normally in important areas of your life, such as work, relationships, or hobbies, outside of your daily routine?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my work is perfectly fine. I function at a very high level, honestly. Just last week I completely restructured the data intake process for my team. 

Actually, speaking of work, the new project management software they forced us to adopt this month is a complete nightmare. They migrated everyone to this cloud-based platform that supposedly integrates with our email clients, but the API polling rate is set to a static fifteen-minute interval. It’s absurd! If you have a time-sensitive data set coming through, you're sitting there waiting for the server handshake while the actual database is already populated. I ended up writing a custom script just to bypass their user interface and query the backend directly, which saves me about forty-five minutes a day. I tried explaining the latency issue to the IT director, but he just told me it was 'company policy' to use the front-end dashboard. It’s just incredible how people accept such sub-optimal workflows without even questioning the underlying mechanics. 

But... wait, what were you asking? Oh, if my routines make it hard to function. No, not at all. Like I said, I'm doing my job better than most of the people in my department. So, no, I haven't really noticed my structure getting in the way of my actual life.

Which I certainly didn't eat. 

But, um... where was I? Right, the anxiety. The thing is, if I do end up having a normal dinner like that, or a restaurant meal, the next morning is... well, it's very distressing. If I step on the scale and it's up even just a single pound, I feel this sharp panic. It just hits me that I’ve completely lost control of the variables, and I feel like I absolutely have to correct it the next day to get the numbers back to where they should be.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's concerns about weight and control significantly interfere with her ability to function in important areas of life outside of her routine, as required for a diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00).
doctor.question: Would you say that your concerns about food, weight, or control have made it difficult for you to function normally in important areas of your life, such as work, relationships, or hobbies, outside of your daily routine?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about functional impairment (difficulty functioning in work, relationships, hobbies), which the patient already answered in a previous turn. None of the remaining symptom manifestations (S043, S044, S046, S084) directly address this question.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my work is perfectly fine. I function at a very high level, honestly. Just last week I completely restructured the data intake process for my team. 

Actually, speaking of work, the new project management software they forced us to adopt this month is a complete nightmare. They migrated everyone to this cloud-based platform that supposedly integrates with our email clients, but the API polling rate is set to a static fifteen-minute interval. It’s absurd! If you have a time-sensitive data set coming through, you're sitting there waiting for the server handshake while the actual database is already populated. I ended up writing a custom script just to bypass their user interface and query the backend directly, which saves me about forty-five minutes a day. I tried explaining the latency issue to the IT director, but he just told me it was 'company policy' to use the front-end dashboard. It’s just incredible how people accept such sub-optimal workflows without even questioning the underlying mechanics. 

But... wait, what were you asking? Oh, if my routines make it hard to function. No, not at all. Like I said, I'm doing my job better than most of the people in my department. So, no, I haven't really noticed my structure getting in the way of my actual life.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a long-standing pattern of restrictive eating driven by an intense fear of gaining weight and a need for control, resulting in significantly low body weight and marked distress when deviating from rigid dietary rules. There is significant preoccupation with body shape and weight, with self-worth closely tied to maintaining a controlled, low weight. While there are elements of anxiety and stress-related symptoms, the clinical picture aligns most closely with anorexia nervosa, restricting type, rather than adjustment disorder or other stress-related conditions.
